{{Short description|Use of colours to indicate a status}}
A '''traffic light rating system''' is a system for indicating the status of a variable using the red, amber or green of [[traffic light]]s.

== Product labelling ==

=== Food and drink ===
Food may be labelled with a '''traffic light label''' showing how much  [[fat]], [[saturated fat]]s, [[sugar]] and [[salt]] are in that food by using the [[traffic light]] signals for high (''red''), medium (''amber'') and low (''green'') percentages for each of these ingredients. Foods with 'green' indicators are healthier and to be preferred over those with 'red' ones.<ref>{{citation
|url=http://www.eatwell.gov.uk/foodlabels/trafficlights/
|title=Traffic light labelling
|accessdate=4 April 2009
|publisher=[[Food Standards Agency]]}}</ref> The label is on the front of the package and easier to spot and interpret than [[Guideline Daily Amount]] (GDA) labelling which will continue. The GDA is difficult to understand for many, including children, and does not lend itself to quick comparisons.  The use of traffic light labelling is supported by many physician groups including the British Medical Association and welcomed by consumers.<ref name=bbc/> Despite worries from some in the food industry that red foods would be shunned, the [[British Medical Association]], [[Food Standards Agency]] and others agree that consumers interpret the labels sensibly and realise they can have red foods as a treat, and these labels are easier to understand than lists of percentages.<ref name=bbc>{{citation
|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/health/6397187.stm
|publisher=[[BBC News]]
|title=Public want food 'traffic lights'
|last=Brimelow|first=Adam
|date=27 February 2007
|access-date=4 April 2009}}</ref>

Currently the traffic light label is used in some European countries on a voluntary basis.

=== Other labelling ===
{{See also|European Union energy label}}
[[White goods]] must be labelled with a [[European Union energy label|label]] indicating energy consumption. This is not strictly a 'traffic light' but by analogy a scale of seven values that run from red to green through intermediate colours.

The system may also be used for the European Game Information System ([[PEGI]]),<ref>{{citation
|url=http://www.mcvuk.com/news/32426/PEGI-ratings-could-be-legal-standard-by-2010
|title=PEGI ratings could be legal standard by 2010
|first1=Michael|last1=French
|first2=Tim|last2=Ingham
|accessdate=2009-04-04
|date=20 November 2008
|publisher=MCV Online
}}</ref> which puts age ratings onto [[video game]]s. Again this is not strictly a 'traffic light' since there are likely to be more than three colours.

==Performance monitoring==
In many factories, different stations on the production line(s) are equipped with factory monitoring and control systems; attached to such systems is a 'traffic light' status indicator which is generally visible from many places within the factory.  Green typically indicates normal levels of production; amber indicates that production has slowed (or attention is otherwise warranted); red indicates that production has stopped or the line is down.{{cn|date=May 2023}}

In the [[British Civil Service]] and other [[departments of the United Kingdom government]], traffic light colours are used as a coding system for good or bad performance, usually known as a 'RAG rating'—Red, Amber, Green. For example, a red workload performance would mean inadequate, amber would mean reasonable, and green would mean good. The letters R, A and G are used in addition to swatches of colour, so that the system can be used by [[colour blindness|colour-blind]] readers.{{cn|date=May 2023}}

===Project management===
When status reporting how well a [[milestone]], [[project]], [[programme management|program]] or [[project portfolio management|portfolio]] is performing or being delivered, [[project manager]]s often use a RAG rating to indicate how [[Project management triangle|on track]] or [[Risk management|at risk]] is the project, its [[deliverable]]s or [[Task (project management)|tasks]].<ref>{{citation |url=http://www3.imperial.ac.uk/ictprojectprocess/pmtools/ragstatus1 |title=RAG Status |accessdate=6 July 2012 |publisher=[[Imperial College London]] }}</ref>

In some cases, additional colours are adopted to communicate nuances of status. For example, blue to show where milestones or components of a milestone, project, programme, or portfolio are complete—referred to as BRAG (Creator: Sam Rafferty).<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://davidjcmorris.com/2012/07/how-to-communicate-status-with-colour/|title=How to communicate status with colour (RAG report)|date=2012-07-10|work=Lean Business Change|access-date=2018-10-17|language=en-US}}</ref>

==Behavioural==
Some organisations, such as the [[U.S. Navy]], use traffic light terminology for [[sexual harassment]] education. Green light behaviour is normal discussions or actions, such as discussing work or assisting someone on stairs. Amber light behaviour is potentially offensive behavior, such as sexist jokes or patting someone on the behind. Red light behaviour is obvious sexual harassment such as sexual requests.{{cn|date=May 2023}}

Various [[Cafeteria|school cafeterias]] in the United States also use a traffic light like device to monitor noise levels among students. A green light means that students are talking quietly, an amber light means that noise is increasing and that the pupils need to quiet down. At a red light, pupils voices are too loud and the device will emit a loud beeping sound to warn the students to stop talking. A red light can also result in disciplinary action from teachers such as reduced [[Recess (break)|recess]] time.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Signaling an End to Classroom, Cafeteria Chatter {{!}} Education World |url=https://www.educationworld.com/a_admin/admin/admin336.shtml |access-date=2022-05-20 |website=www.educationworld.com}}</ref>
